name: Dark Blue
lede: Dark blue is the dark end of blue, and for much of history it was not a separate color at all: the word that gave us indigo and lilac first meant dark blue, and the Greeks counted blue as a kind of darkness.

sections.title: Which dark blue?
sections.body:
Dark blue is a description, not a single color, and our library holds several of them. The swatch on this page, #00008B, is the CSS color `darkblue`: red and green at zero and blue at 139 out of 255 [1]. In ISCC-NBS terms it reads as a vivid purplish blue, 8.2 CIEDE2000 units from that block's center [1]. Our library files International Klein Blue, Ultramarine, Navy Blue and Duke Blue as near-duplicates of it, all within 2.3 units [1].

Other sources use the same words for very different colors. Ridgway's *Dark Blue* (1912) is a greyed #51597B, a scan of an aged plate, and xkcd's survey gives #00035B and #030764, much blacker than the CSS value [1]. The CSS value is a pure screen primary, far more saturated than the grey-blue of Ridgway's plate [1].

sections.title: Nila: a word for dark blue
sections.body:
Much of the world's blue vocabulary begins with a word that simply meant dark blue. Balfour-Paul reports that the Sanskrit *nila*, meaning dark blue, spread east into Southeast Asia and west through Persia and the Arab world, probably along pre-Islamic trade routes and then with the Islamic trade in the dye [3]. Finlay says indigo cultivation reached back more than five thousand years in the Indus Valley, where the plant was called by that word, and that a Babylonian tablet of dye recipes from the seventh century BC shows indigo used in Mesopotamia [4].

The Pigment Compendium traces the chain: *nilah* became Persian *nila*, then Arabic *al-nil*, and from the seventeenth century the Portuguese and French *anil* meant indigo [5]. Paterson notes that *anil* is also the root of the word *lilac* [6]. The Greek-derived name for the dye, *indikon*, meant a substance from India [3]. In other words [[indigo]] and [[lilac]] both come from a word that first meant simply dark blue, and the dye named itself after the color.

sections.title: Blue as a kind of dark
sections.body:
Ancient writers often treated dark blue as a degree of darkness. Coles notes that the Greek word that took in blue was *melas*, which meant dark, and that blue was seen as a value of darkness [7]. Pastoureau adds that *kyaneos*, the root of modern *cyan*, almost always designated a dark color, but that it might as easily be dark blue as purple, black or brown [8]. Ball, summarizing the Greek view, says that blue was dark with a little light added [9].

None of this means the Greeks and Romans could not see blue; that is an old myth [10]. Pastoureau says the controversy rests only on vocabulary, and that scientific texts of antiquity show a good understanding of how color is perceived [10]. The Romans, he adds, were not blind to blue but indifferent or hostile to it: it was the color of barbarians who dyed their bodies with woad, and Pastoureau relays Pliny's assertion that Breton women painted their bodies dark blue, a claim to treat with caution [10].

Ball offers a biological reason why the blue end of the spectrum may look dark. The cones that respond to blue light are the least sensitive of the three types, so fully saturated blue looks relatively dark [9].

sections.title: Dark blue as a near black
sections.body:
For centuries dark blue and black were hard to tell apart. Pastoureau reports that until the late Middle Ages the blacks produced by European dyers were rarely beautiful: often more brown than black, or grey, or dark blue, they covered cloth unevenly and gave clothes a soiled look [11]. Before blue gained prominence in the twelfth century, he adds, dark blue was often considered equivalent to black, a semi-black used for painting hell and demons [11].

A Romanesque example is the painted ceiling of the church at Zillis in Switzerland, from about 1120-25, where the devil's fur is a dark blue that is almost black [11]. Pastoureau says Romanesque artists could make a devil any color as long as it was dark [11].

Dyers found the dark blues hard to manage. Garfield describes a woad vat that, skillfully run, could dye 220 pounds of wool a week, and yield four hundred pounds of dark blue wool in six weeks [12]. Even then, the quality of woad was uncertain, and the dark blues depended on it [12]. Painters had the same problem: Pastoureau says that neither [[gem:lapis-lazuli|lapis lazuli]], azurite nor smalt could make large areas of dense dark blue, and that a blue both dark and reflective was possible only for accents and details [13].

sections.title: Uniforms and political blue
sections.body:
The great shift came with new dyes and new pigments. Pastoureau writes that in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries painters came to value dark blue shades, helped by [[prussian-blue]], a dense dark blue tending toward blue-black with a bronze sheen at high concentration, in Coles's description [13][7]. Indigo, which could dye cloth in the dark blues, was strictly controlled in many countries at that time [13].

Armies adopted the color. Prussian soldiers had worn dark blue since the late seventeenth century, Pastoureau notes, at a time when French and other regiments were multicolored [14]. In France, the blue of the Parisian National Guard was declared the national blue in June 1790, and decrees of late 1792 and early 1793 made it obligatory for the Republic's soldiers [14]. Balfour-Paul links the British naval uniform to indigo as well, saying that Britain adopted an indigo navy blue uniform with white facings in 1745 [15]. The 1745 date is the only precise one we found for [[navy]], so treat it as one author's account [15].

Pastoureau notes that blue is now the most popular dress color in Western Europe, ahead of white, black and beige [14].

sections.title: What the color was said to mean
sections.body:
Because dark blue carried so much weight, writers have attached claims to it. Birren records an old occult belief that dark blue in a person's aura signals religious feeling, and a therapeutic one that clear dark blues soothe the blood and organs [16]. These are old beliefs, not modern evidence, and Birren presents them as such [16]. He also reports that two researchers found the European malaria mosquito alighted most on dark blue, red and brown, and least on yellow, orange and white [16].

Kandinsky, writing in 1912, compared dark blue to the cello and darker still to the double bass, a comparison Gage places in a long line of analogies between color and music [17].

Language also divides the blues. Batchelor notes that Russian has two basic words, one for dark blue and one for light blue, which Russians regard as different colors [18]. Paterson says the same [6]. English has no equivalent basic word, and Batchelor points out that its language gives the parts of blue no such independence [18].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
We looked for this swatch in 23,781 museum paintings [19]. No painting carries it on at least five per cent of the canvas within a CIEDE2000 distance of six, as photographed [19]. On the looser lens of our graph, it appears in just 3 paintings, about 0.01 per cent, which makes it rarer than 79 per cent of the named colors [20]. The earliest is a work of 1775 by Richard Crosse [20]. Photographs of aged, varnished paintings are a poor test of a pigment, and a pure #00008B blue is very unlike any historical dye [19].

The phrase tells a different story. In Google Books, *dark blue* stood at about 31 per cent of its modern peak in 1800, 71 per cent in 1880, 63 per cent in 1920, 46 per cent in 1960 and 57 per cent in 2000, peaking in the 2010s [21]. The count covers every sense of the words, including the sky, the sea and uniforms [21].

openers: Indigo and lilac both come from a word that meant simply dark blue.
